analysis.one_liner: Bans corporal punishment, including paddling and chemical sprays, in schools that receive federal money.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 with only Democratic support, the bill sat in the Senate education committee for the entire two-year Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any school that receives federal money to allow teachers, school staff, police officers, or security guards to physically punish students — including spanking, paddling, painful positions, chemical sprays, and stun guns. Students could sue, the Education Department could withhold federal funds, and the Attorney General could sue schools that kept the practice. The bill would also require states to report on school discipline and would offer grants to help schools switch to positive behavioral supports instead. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved again before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in the states where corporal punishment remains legal — the bill would bar their schools from paddling, spanking, or spraying them, and give them and their parents a way to sue when it happens. Students of color and students with disabilities, who national data show receive a disproportionate share of physical discipline, are a central focus of the bill's enforcement and reporting provisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students in states where paddling is legal

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits program personnel, law enforcement officers, and school security guards from subjecting students to corporal punishment in any program receiving federal financial assistance [S3].
Gives students and parents a private right of action for attorneys' fees, injunctive relief, and compensatory damages against programs that subject them to corporal punishment [S3].

Requires schools to notify parents, the state education agency, and local law enforcement within 24 hours of any use of corporal punishment, with extra notice to disability protection and advocacy systems for students with disabilities [S3].

Authorizes the Education Department to withhold federal funds or issue cease-and-desist orders against noncompliant programs, and requires state education agencies to submit school climate reports and written assurances about compliance [S3].

Authorizes three-year grants to states for positive behavioral interventions, restorative justice, trauma-informed care, and staff training, with priority to schools where suspensions, arrests, and law-enforcement referrals fall disproportionately on students of color and students with disabilities [S3].
Extends the prohibition to schools operated or funded by the Department of Defense and the Department of the Interior, including Bureau of Indian Education schools [S3].

analysis.who_pays: School districts — especially the roughly twenty states that still permit corporal punishment — would bear compliance, reporting, training, and litigation costs, and could lose federal funds for noncompliance. Taxpayers would fund the new grant program, which is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' with no fixed cap.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state and local control over classroom discipline in the states that still permit corporal punishment, a federalism objection that is likely why it drew no Republican support [S3, S4].
The private right of action, with attorneys' and expert fees, exposes school districts to lawsuits whose costs ultimately fall on local taxpayers [S3].

Withholding federal education funding is the main enforcement tool against noncompliant schools, which could reduce services for the very students the bill is meant to protect if a district is slow to comply [S3].
The grant program to help schools adopt alternatives is authorized at an open-ended amount, adding uncapped new federal spending [S3].

The prohibition covers chemical sprays and stun guns used by police officers and security guards in schools, and some school safety advocates argue this leaves staff fewer tools in violent incidents; the bill does preserve officers' ability to carry out lawful duties under other law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending state-sanctioned physical punishment of children in schools — is significant and targeted at a practice that a large majority of states have already banned on their own. The real costs are honest ones: litigation exposure for districts, the risk that funding penalties hurt students at a noncompliant school before it changes course, and open-ended grant spending. The strongest good-faith objection is the federalism one, that discipline policy belongs to states and school boards. On balance, the bill's costs are compliance and implementation costs, while its benefit is protection from physical harm that current federal law does not address.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on May 30, 2023, joined by Senators Brown, Casey, Durbin, Sanders, and Van Hollen [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote [S1, S5].
All seven cosponsors beyond the original sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders; no Republican senator ever signed on [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill; any successor legislation would have to be reintroduced from scratch [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: School systems in the states that still allow corporal punishment keep the practice and avoid the bill's compliance, reporting, and litigation costs, and no new federal grant spending was created. Students in those states gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill's lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors on day one

for.name: Democratic cosponsors (Sens. Brown, Casey, Durbin, Sanders, Van Hollen, plus 7 later cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Signed on to the bill; all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Senator Sanders (Independent)

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for education bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 30, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing or markup, keeping it from any vote for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill or helped move it, leaving the bill with a purely Democratic and Independent base of support

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the Independent Senator Sanders — 13 total, zero Republicans — and the bill died in a committee without ever producing a floor vote to test broader support.

industries.industry: Public school districts (especially in the ~20 states still permitting corporal punishment)
industries.note: Districts that still use paddling would lose the practice and gain compliance, reporting, training, and lawsuit costs, with federal funding at risk for noncompliance. Their interest in keeping physical punishment runs against students' bodily safety, which is exactly what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Education training and consulting providers (positive behavioral intervention, restorative justice, trauma-informed care programs)
industries.note: The bill's grant program would fund training and technical assistance for schools adopting alternatives to physical and exclusionary discipline, creating a funded demand for these providers. The money flows through state education agencies to support the same student-safety goal.

industries.industry: School-based law enforcement and security (school resource officers and security guards)
industries.note: The bill extends the ban to law enforcement officers and security guards in schools, covering chemical sprays and stun guns used on students, while preserving officers' lawful duties under other law. Their interest in keeping force options runs against the students the bill protects.
